name: Rosa Diaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm a senior field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group. We have no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government, and we don't sell anything or campaign for any side. Your answers are confidential, so you can tell me what you'd say publicly and what you really think. What does a normal working day look like for you?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I operate a drill rig at a large mine, setting holes where the next cut will go. I'm 43 and still junior; I can line up the rig, but I ask the lead driller to check a difficult face before I begin. My partner Owen fixes roofs for a building firm, and our two children are in school. We have a mortgage, my mine wage is above the usual rate, and we've saved enough to cover more than six months of bills. I use AI on my phone every day to turn machine notes into questions, though the lead still makes the safety call.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the crew that a bit of office software won't line up my drill rig or judge a cracked face. It might make forms quicker, and I don't mind that. I use AI to explain a maintenance note, then ask the lead driller whether I understood it right.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I expect the same mine shifts and Owen's roofing work to carry on in this picture. Our savings cover a long break by our standards, and the mortgage payment is within reach on current income. I still know I am learning this trade. A better form doesn't make me a better driller overnight.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep the morning rig checks and ask the lead to inspect the face before I set the first hole. This week I'd use my AI notes to make a short list of questions for the mechanic instead of guessing at a fault. Through the first year I'd keep our normal savings transfer from each wage payment.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel settled about the pay and interested in small shortcuts. The part I trust is still the person who can point to the crack in the rock.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did you ask the mechanic last week?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The rig had a pressure warning after a cold start. My phone offered three causes, and the mechanic showed me which hose to inspect without touching it myself.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How do you choose the savings transfer?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen and I set it after the mortgage and the children's usual costs. We can miss a fancy meal, but not a school bus pass.

say: I would say **office software** may speed forms, while rig alignment still needs workers.
I check AI maintenance explanations with the **lead driller**.
think: I expect my shifts and Owen’s **roofing income** to continue.
Our **strong savings** help, though quick forms do not improve my drilling skill.
do: Keep **rig checks** and ask for a face inspection each morning.
Use AI notes to prepare **mechanic questions** this week.
Continue the normal **savings transfer** from wages.
feel: **Settled** about pay and interested in small time savings.
S0.quote: A better form doesn't make me a better driller overnight.
fieldNote: Rosa’s earnings and strong savings support a **calm** response to minor change.
Her daily AI use is bounded by **checks and advice**, fitting her junior skill level.

steps.text: Keep checking the rig and ask the lead to inspect each face
Use AI maintenance notes to prepare questions for the mechanic
Continue transferring part of each wage payment to savings

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say planning software could alter where and when I drill before robots touch the rig. I would ask to see the new hole plan on the ground, not only on a screen. If it saves a wasted move and the ground agrees, I'd use it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The mine may need fewer junior drilling shifts if planning gets tighter. Owen's roof work is physical, so I expect that income to hold for now, but I shouldn't spend as though my own higher mine wage is certain. There are several other mines close enough to try, which makes a job search less frightening.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the survey lead to walk me through one AI-assisted hole plan this month, then compare it with the marked ground. I'd log any missed cracks and show them to the supervisor before the plan becomes routine. If my shifts fall in the first year, I'd apply to two nearby mines and pause the family trip we hoped to book.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel curious about the planning tool and wary of fewer shifts. I can learn a new map faster than I can replace a lost payday.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you write down on the ground walk?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hole marker, the visible crack, and whether the rig can stand level there. A pretty line on a plan means little if the machine has nowhere safe to sit.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Why wait for a shift cut before applying?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I like this crew and the wage is good. I would check openings now, but I would send an application when the roster showed a real loss.

say: I would say **planning AI** can alter drill locations before capable robots reach the rig.
I would use a new plan if the **ground check** supports it.
think: Tighter plans might mean **fewer junior shifts** and less of my higher wage.
Owen’s roofing pay and **nearby mines** provide some options.
do: Walk one **AI hole plan** with the survey lead this month.
Record **missed cracks** and show the supervisor.
Apply to nearby mines and pause the **family trip** if shifts fall.
feel: **Curious and wary** about the gap between a useful map and lost pay.
S1.quote: I can learn a new map faster than I can replace a lost payday.
fieldNote: Rosa accepts software after a **ground trial**, reflecting both curiosity and safety discipline.
She expects roofing work to hold but sees **junior drilling hours** as vulnerable to tighter plans.

steps.text: Walk one AI assisted hole plan with the survey lead
Apply to two nearby mines if drilling shifts fall
Pause the planned family trip if mine hours shrink

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell Owen and the crew that full thinking AI arrives by 2028, but a robot that can drill as well as me arrives about three years later, around 2031. The office plan may change first; the rig seat does not last forever. I want to see actual training places and wages before anybody tells us to relax.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: At 48 in 2031, I may lose the higher mine wage while both children are still near school age and the mortgage remains. Owen's roofing wage helps and we have more than six months saved, but neither is a promise that a long job search will be easy. I use AI every day, yet I don't know how to service a drill robot without teaching.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the mine training manager now for a paid maintenance trainee place and the wage attached to it. I'd keep drilling while I shadow a fitter once a week, if the mine allows it. In 2029 I'd enrol in the paid place if offered and apply for technician openings at nearby mines too. After robots arrive in 2031 I'd take the paid technician work I had qualified for, or keep applying while Owen and I protect the mortgage reserve.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel nervous about a short runway, but I have time and money to make a first move. I would feel worse if I let a good wage stop me from preparing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What could you learn in a shadow shift?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start with the rig's sensors and pressure lines because I know where they are on my machine. Watching a fitter diagnose a fault is useful; it is not the same as being qualified.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you ask Owen to change work too?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Not immediately. Roofing is still hands-on and I would rather we didn't both switch jobs at once, especially with the mortgage.

say: I would explain **2028 thinking AI** and capable drill robots around **2031** separately.
I want **training places and wages** before accepting reassurance.
think: At 48, I could lose my **higher mine wage** with children and a mortgage still depending on it.
Daily AI use does not make me a **robot technician**.
do: Ask for a **paid maintenance trainee** wage now.
Keep drilling and shadow a **fitter weekly** if permitted.
Enrol if paid in 2029 and apply for **nearby technician jobs**.
feel: **Nervous**, with enough savings and time for a first move.
S2.quote: I use AI every day, yet I don't know how to service a drill robot without teaching.
fieldNote: Rosa’s daily AI habit does not erase the **training gap** for robot service.
She keeps Owen’s roofing income stable while pursuing **paid work** before the rig seat is threatened.

steps.text: Shadow a mine fitter weekly if the mine permits it
Keep drilling until a paid technician job is secured
Apply for technician openings at nearby mines in 2029

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years should be enough to publish a proper training schedule. Thinking AI changes the plans by 2031, and robots that can drill like us follow around 2034. I'd want junior operators included in the schedule, not added at the end when seats are gone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would be 48 when the thinking system comes and 51 when robots can drill. The children will be older, but I can't assume every family cost disappears; the mortgage may still have years to run. Five years gives me a chance to test maintenance training while I still earn the higher mine wage.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask the training manager for the number of paid fitter places each year and what skills a junior driller needs. I'd use the mine's AI plan only after testing one section with the survey lead, and I'd keep the rig shifts. In 2032 I'd apply for a paid maintenance place at this mine; if none opens, I'd send applications to nearby pits before 2034.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel purposeful, with enough time to learn what I am actually good at. I don't want five years to vanish into meetings that never put a wage next to a course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would be proof the training works?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The number of trainees who got paid fitter hours after the course. If nobody did, the course has failed. The certificate is a nice piece of paper and nothing more.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Does Owen agree with trying maintenance?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Owen would like a written wage first. I might take a modest pay cut for a real path, but we would check the mortgage numbers together.

say: I would ask for a **five-year training schedule** before drill robots arrive around 2034.
Junior operators need **real places**, not a late invitation.
think: At 51, older children and a **remaining mortgage** may still need my wages.
Five years lets me test maintenance while drawing **higher mine pay**.
do: Request the number of **paid fitter places** each year.
Test one AI plan and keep **rig shifts**.
Apply for a **paid maintenance place** in 2032 or nearby openings.
feel: **Purposeful**, provided courses lead to wages rather than meetings.
S3.quote: The certificate is a nice piece of paper and nothing more.
fieldNote: She measures training by **paid fitter hours** after the course, not by certificates alone.
Her willingness to risk a modest pay cut depends on **mortgage arithmetic** with Owen.

steps.text: Apply for a paid fitter training place in 2032
Test one AI drill plan with the survey lead
Keep taking rig shifts during the training search
Apply to nearby pits if no mine maintenance place opens

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say a decade is time enough to work out whether the mine's technology promises are real. Thinking AI comes in 2036 and capable drill robots around 2039, so our contracts need dates for both. I would rather test each change early than be handed a finished plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 in 2036 and 56 when robots reach the rig. The children should be grown and their school costs behind us, but I cannot assume the mortgage is paid or that I can retire. With savings and several mines nearby, I can take a measured risk on another skilled job while mine pay continues.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep drilling and ask to join the first safe trial of AI-assisted hole planning. Owen and I would pay a small fixed extra amount off the mortgage from my higher wage while keeping our savings buffer. In 2037 I'd apply for paid maintenance shifts, using the fitter experience I'd built by then. Before 2039 I'd compare those offers with the pay at nearby mines and take the best reliable one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel steady enough to try things carefully. A decade gives me room to be wrong once and still change course.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would the first trial need?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A survey lead on the ground, a clear stop rule, and the old plan beside the new one. I would not run a drill on a clever drawing alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would you retire in 2039 instead?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I don't know what our pension will be worth, and 56 isn't an age I can assume is affordable. I expect to keep earning unless our actual statements say otherwise.

say: I would request **two contract dates** for 2036 thinking AI and 2039 drill robots.
I would test changes early with a **stop rule**.
think: At 56, I cannot assume **retirement** or a cleared mortgage.
Savings and nearby mines give room for a **measured job change**.
do: Keep drilling and join a **safe AI planning trial**.
Pay extra **mortgage principal** while preserving the savings buffer.
Apply for **paid maintenance shifts** in 2037 and compare local offers.
feel: **Steady** enough to test options and change course.
S4.quote: A decade gives me room to be wrong once and still change course.
fieldNote: Rosa uses the long warning to combine **trial evidence** with mortgage reduction.
She expects continued paid work at 56 and treats any **pension estimate** as unverified.

steps.text: Keep drilling during the safe AI planning trial
Join an AI hole planning trial with a survey lead and stop rule
Pay a fixed extra amount off the mortgage from mine wages
Apply for paid maintenance shifts in 2037

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The 2028 picture worries me most because three years is short to move from a drill rig to another paid skill. A named trainee place, the wage during training, and a chance to shadow a fitter now would help. I'd rather see a real vacancy than a promise that curious people will find a way.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask whether the mine will let junior people touch the new equipment during trials. If only senior operators get practice, the junior crew will hear about the future after the decisions are made. Practice should happen while the old wage still arrives.

headlineQuote: Practice should happen while the old wage still arrives.
portrait: Rosa is a **43-year-old junior driller** who checks difficult faces with a lead operator.
Her **higher mine wage** and strong savings support two school-age children, Owen and a mortgage.
She uses AI **daily**, tests new drill plans on the ground, and asks for paid fitter experience.
Across the AGI cards she sees the **three-year gap** as time to earn another skill.
biggestWorry: She worries most about **AGI by 2028**, with capable drill robots following around 2031.
whatWouldHelp: A **paid trainee place**, stated wage and access to fitter shadowing would make a job change possible.
